title: How the Sun Shines: Fusion in Its Core
post_title: How the Sun Shines: Fusion in Its Core | QuantaTale
post_description: How hydrogen fuses into helium in the Sun's core and releases energy, from NASA and ESA. Sources: National Aeronautics and Space Administration https://science.nasa.gov/sun/facts/ and European Space Agency https://sci.esa.int/web/education/-/36828-stellar-processes-and-evolution #Science #ScienceFacts #QuantaTale
narration: What keeps the Sun glowing year after year? Deep in the Sun's core, it is hot enough to sustain nuclear fusion. In fusion, small atomic nuclei combine to make a bigger one. In stars like the Sun, the simplest reaction turns hydrogen into helium. The helium that forms has slightly less mass than the hydrogen it came from. The small amount of mass that goes missing is released as energy. Fusion also pushes outward, which stops the Sun from collapsing under its own weight. Most life on our planet depends on that energy.

sources.supports: Nuclear fusion, where nuclei combine to make a nucleus with a larger number of protons and neutrons, occurs in main sequence stars once they reach a critical temperature. | The simplest reaction that occurs in stars is the conversion of hydrogen into helium - a process known as the proton-proton chain and requires a core temperature of at least 10 million K. | Each helium-4 nucleus has a mass that is about 99.3% of the mass of four protons. | The missing 4 million tons of matter is released as energy in accordance with Einstein's equation E=mc 2 .
